rationale: Matthew 18:8-9 repeats, with changes, the sayings Matthew already gave at 5:29-30. In this app's BSB, "gouge it out and throw it away" occurs only at 5:29 and 18:9, and "cut it off and throw it away" only at 5:30 and 18:8 (script searches). In Greek the eye clause is the same in both places, "ho ophthalmos sou ... skandalizei se, exele auton kai bale apo sou," except that 5:29 adds "the right" (ho dexios), and both hand sayings use ekkopson and bale apo sou (SBL and Byzantine texts on Bible Hub). The differences are checkable: 18:8 adds the foot, and both 18:8 and 18:9 drop "right"; 5:29-30 end in "hell" (geenna), 18:8 in "the eternal fire" and 18:9 in "the fire of hell" (BSB footnote: "Greek the Gehenna of fire"); 5:29-30 speak of losing "one part of your body" and 18:8-9 of entering "life" crippled, lame or with one eye; and the setting moves from lust (5:28) to causing others to stumble (18:6-7). A saying repeated within one Gospel is why the type is motif, following conn-matt16-sign-matt12, and the shared, distinctive wording is why the label is strong. Calvin notes the repetition ("As those two verses have been already explained ... under Matthew 5:29,30"), and the Expositor's Greek Testament calls the verses "one of Mt.'s dualities." The row grades the repetition, not what the sayings require; that is reported in the lesson's Positions, and lesson 11 (Matthew 5:21-48) covers the first occurrence.
